summary: Provides terminology and methodology for benchmarking next-generation network security devices, such as next-generation firewalls and intrusion prevention systems. It covers test configuration parameters and testing approaches.

plainLanguage.summary: Firewall and intrusion-prevention products are sold on speed figures, but those figures only mean something if everyone measures in the same way. This memo sets out one way to measure them: the same lab, the same settings, the same traffic, and the same numbers reported at the end.

questions: how to benchmark a next-generation firewall
what is a device under test
what is the sustain phase in a benchmark
subtitle: How to test the speed of next-generation firewalls and intrusion prevention systems so results can be compared fairly.

tldr.problem: Firewalls grew from simple access-list filters into devices that inspect encrypted traffic and block exploits, and the old test method from 2003 no longer fit them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fixes the test setup, device features, client and server settings and traffic phases, then defines nine benchmarking tests plus a security-effectiveness check with KPIs such as throughput, connections per second and latency.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3511 and is informational: it is a lab method, not a protocol, meant to make vendor results reproducible and comparable.

today: RFC 9411 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 3511, and no later RFC is listed as replacing it. It is a laboratory test method rather than a protocol, and it leaves the technical contents of the devices themselves unchanged.

sections.title: Introduction: Why a New Benchmarking Method
sections.content:
It has been 18 years since the IETF initially recommended test methodology and terminology for firewalls. Firewalls have evolved significantly from the days of simple access control list filters, and as the underlying technology has progressed, the requirements and expectations for network security elements have increased tremendously. Security function implementations have evolved and diversified into intrusion detection and prevention, threat management, analysis of encrypted traffic and more. In an industry of growing importance, well-defined and reproducible key performance indicators are increasingly needed to enable fair and reasonable comparisons of network security functions. Those reasons led to the creation of this document, which makes RFC 3511 obsolete.

The measurement of performance for processing IP-fragmented traffic is not included, because IP fragmentation does not commonly occur in traffic any more, unlike how it might have been when RFC 3511 was written. The document also notes that RFC 2647 retains significant value and was consulted frequently while it was being created.
sections.plainLanguage: The old method was written for a simpler kind of firewall. Since then these devices have taken on work that costs much more processing, so the way they are tested has to be redone from scratch.

sections.title: Scope and What Is Measured
sections.content:
The document provides testing terminology and methodology for modern and next-generation network security devices that are configured in Active, or Inline, mode. It covers the validation of security effectiveness configurations of network security devices, followed by performance benchmark testing. It focuses on advanced, realistic and reproducible testing methods, and additionally describes testbed environments, test tool requirements and test result formats.

The performance testing methodology is not intended for security devices or systems that rely on machine learning or behavioural analysis. If such features are present in a Device Under Test or System Under Test, they should be disabled.

The results are reported as key performance indicators, all of which must be measured during the sustain phase of the traffic load profile and taken from the output of the test equipment. They are: concurrent TCP connections, the aggregate number of simultaneous connections across the device; concurrent QUIC connections; TCP connections per second, the average number of successfully established connections, where the sessions must not be closed by RST; QUIC connections per second; application transactions per second, where a transaction counts as successful only if all the data was transferred in its entirety and, for HTTP, the status code is 200 OK; the TLS handshake rate; inspected throughput, the number of bits per second of examined and allowed traffic the device can transmit to the correct destination interfaces in response to a specified offered load; Time to First Byte, the elapsed time until the client receives the first packet of application data; and URL Response Time, also called Time to Last Byte, the elapsed time until the client receives the last packet of application data.
sections.plainLanguage: Only devices that inspect traffic in line can be tested this way, and any feature that learns from behaviour has to be switched off, because such a feature would make two test runs incomparable.

sections.title: The Test Setup
sections.content:
The test setup applies to all the benchmarking tests and must be contained within an isolated test environment. The testbed configuration must ensure that any performance implications discovered during the benchmark are not due to the inherent physical network limitations, such as the number of physical links and the forwarding performance of the network devices in the testbed, so the document recommends avoiding external devices such as switches and routers wherever possible, and using test equipment able to emulate layer 3 routing instead.

The same device configuration must be used for all the benchmarking tests. Since each device has its own unique configuration, users must configure their devices with the same parameters and security features that would be used in the actual or a typical deployment, and the device must be configured in Inline mode so that traffic is actively inspected. The document lists the recommended and optional sets of security features for next-generation firewalls and for next-generation intrusion prevention systems: TLS inspection, IDS/IPS, anti-spyware, anti-virus, anti-botnet, anti-evasion and application identification are recommended for both, with web filtering, data loss protection, DDoS protection and certificate validation optional for firewalls and deep packet inspection recommended for intrusion prevention systems. If a recommended feature is not enabled, the reason must be reported with the results, and the report must note that not enabling it may affect performance. A summary of the configuration, including all enabled features, must be published with the results to improve repeatability. Fail-open behaviour must be disabled, logging and reporting must be enabled, and geographical location filtering should be configured.

A realistic number of access control lists should be configured where the device supports them, and the document fixes the number of rules for four device classes, from Extra Small to Large, with the rules ordered from most specific to least specific, blocking first and allowing afterwards. The configured rules must not block the test traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things have to be pinned down before any number means anything: the device under test and the security features it has switched on, the lab around it, and the traffic generator's own settings. The document fixes all three, so that two labs running the test get comparable answers.

sections.title: The Traffic Load Profile
sections.content:
Loading traffic has five phases. In the Init phase, the testbed devices negotiate layer 2 and 3 connectivity such as MAC learning and ARP or neighbour discovery, and only after that does the iteration move on; the minimum recommended time is 5 seconds, and the emulated clients must not start any sessions with the device during this phase, while the emulated servers should be ready to accept requests.

In the Ramp Up phase, the test equipment starts to generate the test traffic using an approximate number of unique client IP addresses, and the traffic ramps up from zero to the desired target objective. The duration must be long enough that the equipment does not overwhelm the stated performance metrics of the device, and no measurements are made in this phase.

In the Sustain phase, all required clients are active and operating at their desired load condition, and the equipment continues to generate traffic to a constant target value for a constant number of active clients. The minimum recommended duration is 300 seconds, this is the phase where measurements occur, and the equipment must measure and record statistics continuously with a sampling interval of less than 2 seconds. In the Ramp Down phase the traffic slows to zero with no measurements taken, and the Collection phase is administrative, where the equipment merges and collates the report data.

Before the benchmarking tests start, a reference test controls the environment. The device is configured in the most trivial setup, or left out entirely, traffic is generated with the smallest object size, any ancillary switching or routing added to the test equipment must not limit performance by introducing packet loss or latency, the generated traffic must match and reasonably exceed the expected maximum performance of the device, the packet loss and latency introduced by the environment are recorded, and the stability of the testbed is asserted for the whole session.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic is turned up, held steady, and turned down. Only the steady part is measured, and it has to be held for at least five minutes so that the numbers describe how the device really behaves rather than how it behaves for the first few seconds.

sections.title: The Nine Benchmarking Tests
sections.content:
The tests focus on HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 traffic over TCP; the document does not define specific tests for QUIC or HTTP/3 indicators, but the methodology in the connections per second, latency, throughput and concurrent connection tests with HTTPS traffic can be used for them, and the application traffic mix throughput test can be run with any application traffic, including HTTP/3.

Throughput performance with an application traffic mix determines the sustainable inspected throughput supported by the device, using a mix relevant to the customer's use case, and the report must document the names of the applications and layer 7 protocols, the percentage of emulated traffic for each, the percentage of encrypted traffic with the cipher suites and keys used, and the object sizes used. TCP connections per second with HTTP traffic determines the sustainable connection establishment rate under different load conditions, using different fixed HTTP response object sizes. HTTP throughput determines the sustainable inspected throughput while the HTTP response object size varies, with the recommended response object sizes being 1, 2, 4, 16 and 64 KB. HTTP transaction latency determines the latency while the device runs at its sustainable rate of HTTP transactions per second, with test iterations performed with different object sizes in two scenarios: one with a single transaction per connection, and one with 10 transactions in a single connection.

Concurrent TCP connection capacity with HTTP traffic determines how many concurrent connections the device sustains. TCP or QUIC connections per second with HTTPS traffic determines the sustainable TLS session establishment rate, with test iterations including common cipher suites and key strengths as well as forward-looking stronger keys, and each cipher suite and key strength using a single HTTPS response object size. HTTPS throughput determines the sustainable inspected throughput for HTTPS transactions by varying the response object size. HTTPS transaction latency measures the same way as the HTTP variant, with one transaction or 10 transactions in a single TCP or QUIC connection. Concurrent TCP or QUIC connection capacity with HTTPS traffic determines how many concurrent encrypted connections are sustained.

Every test has the same shape: step one checks that the device can reach the initial throughput, which is 10% of the target inspected throughput, while meeting the validation criteria; step two finds out whether the target value can be reached within the criteria; step three finds the maximum value achievable within the criteria. The criteria are that fewer than 0.001%, that is one out of 100,000, of attempted transactions fail, that fewer than 0.001% of TCP connections are terminated by an unexpected RST from the device, and that, if HTTP/3 is used, fewer than 0.001% of QUIC connections fail because of unexpected error codes.
sections.plainLanguage: There are nine tests: how much traffic the device can push through, how many connections it can open per second, how much it can keep open at once, and how long a request takes, each measured for plain web traffic and for encrypted web traffic.

sections.title: Security Effectiveness and the Security Considerations
sections.content:
Before performance tests, the document recommends validating the security effectiveness of the device configuration by evaluating security effectiveness as a prerequisite. The selected security features must be configured to detect, prevent and report the defined vulnerability sets, selected from the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures list. The vulnerability set should reflect a minimum of 500 CVEs from no older than 10 calendar years to the current year, chosen with a focus on in-use software commonly found in business applications and with a CVSS severity of High, that is 7 to 10. If the performance tests are run without evaluating security effectiveness, the test report must explain the implications. The methodology for evaluating security effectiveness is defined in an appendix, with background traffic followed by CVE emulation.

The security considerations note that readers should be aware of some overlap between performance and security issues, because the optimal configuration for performance may not be the most secure and the reverse is also true. Testing security platforms with working exploits and malware carries risks, so proper access controls must be implemented to prevent unintended exposure to vulnerable networks or systems. The cipher suites recommended in the document are for test purposes only, and the recommendation for a real deployment is out of scope.

Security assessment of a product could also include an analysis of whether unusual traffic characteristics would have a significant impact on performance, since such impacts would let an attacker use crafted traffic as a denial of service attack to reduce the performance available to other traffic. Uncommon characteristics might include IP-fragmented traffic, a specific type of application traffic, or uncommonly high HTTP transaction rate traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A fast device that does not block anything is not a good firewall, so the document expects the security features to be checked first, against a list of several hundred known vulnerabilities. It also warns that a device that drops every unknown connection can be used against itself, because an attacker can send awkward traffic to slow the device down for everyone else.

viz.caption: THE FIVE PHASES OF A TRAFFIC LOAD PROFILE

messages.label: INIT
messages.note: Connectivity is learned. No sessions start and no measurements are taken. Minimum 5 seconds.

messages.label: RAMP UP
messages.note: Traffic rises from zero to the target. No measurements are taken.

messages.label: SUSTAIN
messages.note: Constant load for a constant number of clients. This is where measurements happen. Minimum 300 seconds.

messages.label: RAMP DOWN
messages.note: Traffic slows to zero. No measurements are taken.

messages.label: COLLECTION
messages.note: The report data is merged and collated.

viz.caption: THE NINE BENCHMARKING TESTS AND WHAT EACH ONE FINDS OUT

TCP connections per second with HTTP
The sustainable connection establishment rate under different load conditions
The sustainable inspected throughput for HTTP transactions, by response object size
The time a client waits for an HTTP response at a sustainable transaction rate
How many concurrent connections the device sustains
TCP or QUIC connections per second with HTTPS
The sustainable TLS session establishment rate
The sustainable inspected throughput for HTTPS transactions, by response object size
The time a client waits for an HTTPS response at a sustainable transaction rate
Concurrent TCP or QUIC connections with HTTPS
How many concurrent encrypted connections the device sustains

viz.caption: THE KEY PERFORMANCE INDICATORS THE REPORT MUST CARRY

items.title: Inspected throughput
items.text: The bits per second of examined and allowed traffic the device can send on in response to a given offered load.

items.title: Application transactions per second
items.text: Successfully completed transactions per second. A transaction counts only if all the data was transferred in full and, for HTTP, the status code is 200 OK.

items.title: TCP connections per second
items.text: The average number of successfully established TCP connections per second. Sessions must not be closed by a RST.

items.title: QUIC connections per second
items.text: The average number of successfully established QUIC connections per second.

items.title: Concurrent connections
items.text: The aggregate number of simultaneous TCP or QUIC connections across the device.

items.title: TLS handshake rate
items.text: The average number of successfully established TLS connections per second.

items.title: Time to first byte
items.text: The elapsed time from the client starting the handshake until the first packet of application data arrives.

items.title: Time to last byte
items.text: The elapsed time from the client starting the handshake until the last packet of application data arrives.
